Many tasks come down to doing something to *some* of a graph's nodes or edges: tag the hubs, delete
the weak ties, extract the neighborhood of one node, reverse a set of edges. EdgeCase handles these
with *selections*. A graph holds a current selection, `select_*` methods build it, and methods whose
names end in `_ws` ("with selection") act on it:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec

karate = ec.karate_club()

(
    karate
    .select_nodes_by_degree(min_degree=10)
    .set_node_attrs_ws(hub=True)
    .get_node_df_ws()
)
```

The first call selected the four members with ten or more friends, the second tagged them, and the
third showed the selected rows of the node table. The same two-part pattern, select and then act,
underlies everything on this page.

A selection is part of the graph's state. It persists from one call to the next until something
changes it, which is what lets a selection made in one call be used by the next. The flip side is
that a forgotten selection lingers, so finish with
[`clear_selection()`](../reference/Graph.clear_selection.qmd) when you're done:

```{python}
karate.clear_selection().count_selected_nodes()
```

A graph selects either nodes or edges, never both at once. Selecting edges clears any node
selection, and selecting nodes clears any edge selection.

## Selecting nodes

| Method | Selects |
|---|---|
| [`select_nodes_by_id()`](../reference/Graph.select_nodes_by_id.qmd) | the nodes with the given IDs |
| [`select_nodes()`](../reference/Graph.select_nodes.qmd) | the nodes for which a Python function returns `True` |
| [`select_nodes_by_degree()`](../reference/Graph.select_nodes_by_degree.qmd) | the nodes with a degree in a range |
| [`select_nodes_by_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.select_nodes_by_centrality.qmd) | the top `k` nodes by a centrality measure |
| [`select_nodes_in_neighborhood()`](../reference/Graph.select_nodes_in_neighborhood.qmd) | the nodes within `k` hops of some seed nodes |
| [`select_last_nodes_created()`](../reference/Graph.select_last_nodes_created.qmd) | the most recently added nodes |
| [`select_match()`](../reference/Graph.select_match.qmd) | the nodes that match a Cypher pattern |

### By attribute

[`select_nodes()`](../reference/Graph.select_nodes.qmd) is the most general selector. It calls a
function once for each node, passing a `Node` object with `id`, `label`, and `attributes`, and
selects the nodes for which the function returns `True`. Here it selects the members of the
instructor's faction:

```{python}
karate.select_nodes(lambda node: node.attributes["faction"] == 1)
karate.count_selected_nodes()
```

The function must return an actual `bool`, which guards against a common mistake: in a graph where
some nodes lack an attribute, an expression like `node.attributes.get("score") and ...` can return
`None`, and EdgeCase raises a `TypeError` rather than silently treating it as false. A node with no
attributes at all has `attributes` set to `None`, so for graphs where that can happen, write the
test as `node.attributes is not None and ...`.

### By structure

The specialized selectors run in Rust, so on large graphs they are much faster than an equivalent
`select_nodes()` predicate. [`select_nodes_by_degree()`](../reference/Graph.select_nodes_by_degree.qmd)
selects by degree, and in a directed graph `degree_type=` chooses in-, out-, or total degree.
[`select_nodes_by_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.select_nodes_by_centrality.qmd) selects the
top `k` nodes by degree, PageRank, or betweenness:

```{python}
karate.select_nodes_by_centrality(measure="betweenness", k=3, set_op="replace")
sorted(karate.get_selected_node_ids())
```

The three best brokers are the instructor (ID 1), the administrator (ID 34), and member `"32"`
(ID 33), one of the administrator's closest allies. The `set_op="replace"` argument made these
three the whole selection, rather than adding them to the faction members selected before; see
[Combining selections](#combining-selections) below.

[`select_nodes_in_neighborhood()`](../reference/Graph.select_nodes_in_neighborhood.qmd) selects an
*ego network*: one or more seed nodes and everything within `k` hops of them. This selects the
administrator and all of their friends:

```{python}
karate.select_nodes_in_neighborhood("33", k=1, set_op="replace").count_selected_nodes()
```

### By pattern

[`select_match()`](../reference/Graph.select_match.qmd) selects whatever a Cypher `MATCH` pattern
finds. By default it selects every node in every match; `select=` names the variables to keep. This
selects the members who have a friend in the other faction:

```{python}
karate.select_match(
    "MATCH (a)--(b) WHERE a.faction <> b.faction",
    select="a",
    set_op="replace",
)
karate.count_selected_nodes()
```

[Cypher queries](cypher.qmd) describes the pattern language in full.

## Inspecting a selection

Three methods report on the current node selection:

- [`count_selected_nodes()`](../reference/Graph.count_selected_nodes.qmd) counts it,
- [`get_selected_node_ids()`](../reference/Graph.get_selected_node_ids.qmd) lists its IDs (in no
  particular order, so sort them if the order matters), and
- [`get_node_df_ws()`](../reference/Graph.get_node_df_ws.qmd) returns its rows of the node table.

```{python}
karate.get_node_df_ws().select("id", "label", "faction", "role")
```

Each has an edge counterpart: `count_selected_edges()`, `get_selected_edge_ids()`, and
`get_edge_df_ws()`.

## Combining selections

Every `select_*` method takes a `set_op=` argument that says how its result combines with the
current selection:

| `set_op=` | Result |
|---|---|
| `"union"` (the default) | the current selection plus the new matches |
| `"replace"` | the new matches only |
| `"intersect"` | the current selection, keeping only the new matches |
| `"difference"` | the current selection, without the new matches |

Chaining selectors with these operations builds up compound conditions. This finds the hubs of the
administrator's faction: members with at least six friends, intersected with faction 2:

```{python}
(
    karate
    .select_nodes_by_degree(min_degree=6, set_op="replace")
    .select_nodes(lambda node: node.attributes["faction"] == 2, set_op="intersect")
    .get_node_df_ws()
    .select("id", "label", "faction", "degree")
)
```

The default is `"union"`, so without `set_op="replace"` the first selector would have added to the
members selected by the previous example. Starting each new selection with either
`clear_selection()` or `set_op="replace"` avoids such leftovers.

Three more methods adjust a selection directly.
[`deselect_nodes()`](../reference/Graph.deselect_nodes.qmd) removes some nodes from it,
[`invert_node_selection()`](../reference/Graph.invert_node_selection.qmd) swaps the selected and
unselected nodes, and `clear_selection()` empties it. Removing the seed from an ego network, for
instance, leaves just the neighbors:

```{python}
(
    karate
    .select_nodes_in_neighborhood("33", k=1, set_op="replace")
    .deselect_nodes(["33"])
    .count_selected_nodes()
)
```

## Acting on selected nodes

| Method | Effect |
|---|---|
| [`set_node_attrs_ws()`](../reference/Graph.set_node_attrs_ws.qmd) | set attributes on every selected node |
| [`mutate_node_attrs_ws()`](../reference/Graph.mutate_node_attrs_ws.qmd) | transform an attribute's value on every selected node |
| [`delete_nodes_ws()`](../reference/Graph.delete_nodes_ws.qmd) | delete the selected nodes and their edges |
| [`transform_to_subgraph_ws()`](../reference/Graph.transform_to_subgraph_ws.qmd) | return a new graph of the selected nodes and the edges among them |
| [`fully_connect_nodes_ws()`](../reference/Graph.fully_connect_nodes_ws.qmd) | join every pair of selected nodes with an edge |
| [`get_node_df_ws()`](../reference/Graph.get_node_df_ws.qmd) | return the selected rows of the node table |

`set_node_attrs_ws()` takes the attributes as keyword arguments, so one call can set several, and
`mutate_node_attrs_ws()` applies a function to the current value of one attribute. Together they
make conditional updates easy. Here the PageRank of the two leaders is scaled down, as might be
done to study the network's structure without their dominance:

```{python}
(
    karate
    .pagerank()
    .select_nodes_by_id([1, 34], set_op="replace")
    .set_node_attrs_ws(leader=True, note="scaled")
    .mutate_node_attrs_ws("pagerank", lambda value: value / 2)
    .get_node_df_ws()
    .select("id", "label", "pagerank", "leader", "note")
)
```

`transform_to_subgraph_ws()` extracts the selection as a new graph and leaves the original alone.
Combined with a neighborhood selection, it extracts an ego network:

```{python}
ego = karate.select_nodes_in_neighborhood("0", k=1, set_op="replace").transform_to_subgraph_ws()
ego
```

The nodes keep their IDs, labels, and attributes in the new graph, so results computed on the
subgraph can be matched back to the original.

`delete_nodes_ws()` is the bulk counterpart of `delete_node()`. A common use is pruning, such as
removing every node of degree one before an analysis of the network's core:

```{python}
core = karate.subgraph(karate.get_node_ids(limit=None))
core.select_nodes_by_degree(max_degree=1).delete_nodes_ws()
core.count_nodes()
```

Only one member had a single friend. The deletion was made on a copy, taken with `subgraph()`, so
`karate` itself still has all 34 members.

## Selecting edges

| Method | Selects |
|---|---|
| [`select_edges_by_id()`](../reference/Graph.select_edges_by_id.qmd) | the edges with the given IDs |
| [`select_edges()`](../reference/Graph.select_edges.qmd) | the edges for which a Python function returns `True` |
| [`select_edges_by_node()`](../reference/Graph.select_edges_by_node.qmd) | every edge that touches the given nodes |
| [`select_last_edges_created()`](../reference/Graph.select_last_edges_created.qmd) | the most recently added edges |
| [`select_match()`](../reference/Graph.select_match.qmd) with `select=` naming a relationship variable | the edges that match a Cypher pattern |

[`select_edges()`](../reference/Graph.select_edges.qmd) passes its function an `Edge` object with
`id`, `source`, `target`, `weight`, and `attributes`. A natural use is a weight threshold. In *Les
Misérables*, where the weight counts the chapters two characters share, more than a third of the
pairs meet only once:

```{python}
les_mis = ec.les_miserables()
les_mis.select_edges(lambda edge: edge.weight is not None and edge.weight < 2)
les_mis.count_selected_edges(), les_mis.count_edges()
```

Deleting those single encounters leaves the network of lasting relationships:

```{python}
les_mis.delete_edges_ws()
les_mis.count_edges(), les_mis.count_weakly_connected_components()
```

Removing the 97 weakest edges split the network into 20 pieces, since many minor characters appear
only once beside a main character and are left isolated.

### Acting on selected edges

| Method | Effect |
|---|---|
| [`set_edge_attrs_ws()`](../reference/Graph.set_edge_attrs_ws.qmd) | set attributes on every selected edge |
| [`mutate_edge_attrs_ws()`](../reference/Graph.mutate_edge_attrs_ws.qmd) | transform an attribute's value on every selected edge |
| [`delete_edges_ws()`](../reference/Graph.delete_edges_ws.qmd) | delete the selected edges, keeping their endpoints |
| [`rev_edge_dir_ws()`](../reference/Graph.rev_edge_dir_ws.qmd) | reverse the selected edges (directed graphs only) |
| [`add_reverse_edges_ws()`](../reference/Graph.add_reverse_edges_ws.qmd) | add a reversed copy of each selected edge (directed graphs only) |
| [`transform_to_subgraph_ws()`](../reference/Graph.transform_to_subgraph_ws.qmd) | return a new graph of the selected edges and their endpoints |
| [`get_edge_df_ws()`](../reference/Graph.get_edge_df_ws.qmd) | return the selected rows of the edge table |

The direction methods are useful for fixing data in which some edges were recorded the wrong way
round. In this small dependency graph, the edges should all point from a service to what it depends
on, but the edges into the database were recorded backwards:

```{python}
services = ec.Graph.from_edges(
    [("web", "api"), ("api", "auth"), ("db", "api"), ("db", "auth")],
    directed=True,
)
db = services.get_id_from_label("db")

(
    services
    .select_edges(lambda edge: edge.source == db)
    .rev_edge_dir_ws()
    .set_edge_attrs_ws(rel="depends_on", fixed=True)
    .clear_selection()
)
services.get_edges_str_repr()
```

Both edges out of `db` (ID 4) now point into it. The selection persisted across the two `_ws`
calls, so the same edges were reversed and then tagged.

## Selections, traversals, and plots

Selections are also the starting point for *traversals*, which move a selection along the edges of
the graph: from a set of nodes to their neighbors, to the edges between them, and so on.
[Traversals](traversals.qmd) covers them.

`plot()` doesn't draw the selection itself. To highlight selected nodes in a drawing, store a flag
with `set_node_attrs_ws()` and color by it:

```{python}
(
    karate
    .select_nodes_by_centrality(measure="pagerank", k=5, set_op="replace")
    .set_node_attrs_ws(top5=True)
    .clear_selection()
    .plot(color_by="top5", label_by="label", seed=7)
)
```

Nodes without the attribute form their own color group, so the five most central members stand
apart from the rest.
